## Introduction

In this section, we explore the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), the first step of constructing an operational Structural Causal Model. Though this step seems like a simple drawing exercise, it is critical to the SCM process. This step often becomes one of the most illuminating parts of the SCM process. If done thoroughly and carefully, building the DAG forces you to explicitly state assumptions that you did not realize were critical to your questions. 

## General architecture of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)

A Directed Acyclic Graph represents all plausible causal relationships in your system. In essence, it encapsulates everything important in our study system. This DAG will form the basis for your entire set of questions about your system.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## **Important DAG terminology**

* **node**: a variable in the system (measured or _not_).  
* **edge**: a directed link (unidirectional arrow) representing a causal relationship between two nodes
* **exposure**: the variable whose effect you want to estimate (your treatment or independent variable)
* **outcome**: the variable you are trying to explain (the response or dependent variable) 
* **confounder**: a common cause of both exposure and outcome (can bias the estimate if not accounted for)  
* **mediator**: a variable through which the exposure affects an outcome 
* **collider**: a common effect of two variables (adjusting for it can induce spurious associations)
* **path**: any sequence of connected arrows between two variables
* **backdoor path**: a non-causal path that can introduce bias if not included in the model
* **adjustment set**: the set of variables included in the model (blocking alternative causal pathways and allowing you to recover a causal effect)

:::

The most important aspect of Directed Acyclic Graphs is that they are comprised of nodes (the boxes or circles) connected by edges (lines). In DAGs, edges have directionality (an arrow pointing from $X$ to $Y$ reflects our assumption that $X$ directly causes $Y$). 

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="63%"}
As an example, consider the DAG picture here. It shows conceptual knowledge about what factors affect nest survival. Vegetation cover can influence both predator abundance and survival, while predators affect survival both directly and by influencing how well nests are concealed. In other words, part of the predator effect may work through how hidden the nests are (a behaviorally mediated effect).

Edges in the DAG should be motivated by:

* **ecological theory** (e.g. predator abundance → prey survival)  
* **empirical literature** (e.g. temperature → metabolic rate)  
* **natural history observations** (e.g. insects emerge after rainfall)  
* **experimental design** (e.g. food supplementation → nestling growth)

Typical node categories include:

* **environmental drivers** (e.g. rainfall, temperature)  
* **organismal traits** (e.g. body size, metabolic rate)  
* **behavioral responses** (e.g. foraging rate, vigilance)  
* **demographic outcomes** (e.g. survival, reproductive success)  
* **human dimensions** (e.g., land use, management actions, harvest pressure, recreation)
* **measurement processes** (e.g. detection probability, observer effort)
:::

::: {.column width="2%"}
:::

::: {.column width="35%"}
```{mermaid}
graph TD

C[Vegetation cover]:::node
X[Predator abundance]:::node
M[Nest concealment]:::node
Y[Nest survival]:::node

C --> X
C --> Y
X --> M
M --> Y
X --> Y

classDef node fill:#d9d9d9,color:#000,stroke-width:0px;

```

:::

::::

It is helpful to have an idea of what kinds of roles each node. Here is a useful breakdown of causal roles for different types of nodes:

::: {.course-info}
| Role | Key question | What it is | Include / Include in model? | Example |
|------|-------------|------------|----------------------|---------|
| **Driver** | What generates variation? | Broad upstream cause | Yes, when they are confounders of the focal relationship | Climate, traits |
| **System setup** | What does the system look like at the start? | Initial conditions or state | Usually; they define context and may confound relationships | Density, habitat, distance |
| **Mechanism** | What processes modify the system? | Specific pathways (mediators) | Yes, only when estimating direct effects | Predation, dispersal, mutualists |
| **Outcome** | What are we trying to explain? | Response variable | No, this is the variable being explained | Recruitment, survival |
| **Measurement** | How is it observed? | Observation/detection process | Sometimes include, when correcting for detection or measurement bias | Detection probability, counts |
| **Selection / design** | Why do we observe these data? | Sampling process | Sometimes, because conditioning can induce bias | Plot placement, effort |
:::


Remember that a DAG is a deliberate, simplified representation of a set of causal assumptions about a given study system. Any good DAG should represent **causal assumptions**, _not_ statistical correlations. If there is good ecological justification for a causal link between two variables, you should include it in the model (even if a relationship between two variables has never been tested). Unlike non-causal approaches, a useful DAG emphasizes conceptual completeness over statistical parsimony. In other words, it is better to include more knowledge in a DAG than try to simplify it. So, how do we efficiently construct a DAG that has strong causal assumptions?

## Constructing a DAG for your study system

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## **Rule: Build one DAG for the system -- not one DAG per question/prediction.**
:::

The goal of this section is to construct a _single global Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)_ that represents the causal structure of your study system. I use the term “global” by analogy to multimodel inference (i.e. use of AIC to select the best-supported model) where a global model includes all plausible predictors. In this causal case, a global DAG includes all plausible causal relationships in the system and acknowledges that there can be many outcome/response variables and that variables can play different roles (colliders, mediators, confounders) along multiple causal pathways. A global DAG:

* includes all **relevant variables** (measured and unmeasured)
* represents all **plausible causal relationships**
* integrates **theory, empirical knowledge, and natural history**
* is designed to support **many possible causal questions**

In other words, the goal of DAG construction is not to build a single model; its goal is to thoroughly represent your study system. Once constructed, a global DAG allows you to:

* logically and transparently ask multiple exposure–outcome questions without changing your assumptions about how the world works (what kitchen-sink models and AIC fundamentally do)
* identify confounders, mediators, and colliders
* determine valid adjustment sets (i.e. what covariates should be included in a statistical model)
* convert causal assumptions into statistical models that test predictions  

::: {.callout-important}
## How big should a global DAG be? 

You could easily imagine an ever-expanding (and reductionist) DAG. Certainly, global DAGs can be very large. For purposes of causal identification and modeling for a focal study, a large DAG is not necessary. As you will discover as you gain more experience with this approach, covariates more than two edges away rarely play any important role in answering your set of questions. Therefore, you can construct a DAG that has 1-2 linked covariates away from any dependent variable (called an exposure in the causal world). 

:::

## A practical workflow for building a DAG

Building a DAG for a study system typically involves the following steps. These steps provide **guidelines rather than a rigid sequence**. In practice, DAG construction is iterative: drawing one relationship may cause you to reconsider another, identify a missing variable, or refine how you have represented a biological process.

* **Step 1:** [Start with the study system, not a statistical model](#dag-step-1)
* **Step 2:** [Identify your core exposure–outcome questions](#dag-step-2)
* **Step 3:** [Represent important causal relationships](#dag-step-3)
* **Step 4:** [Look upstream for common causes (confounders)](#dag-step-4)
* **Step 5:** [Look downstream for mechanisms and consequences](#dag-step-5)
* **Step 6:** [Integrate the pieces into a common causal model](#dag-step-6)
* **Step 7:** [Represent underlying processes (latent variables, measurement, and scale)](#dag-step-7)
* **Step 8:** [Refine and interrogate the DAG](#dag-step-8)
* **Step 9:** [Consider effect modification (interactions)](#dag-step-9)
* **Step 10:** [Use the DAG to determine what questions are possible](#dag-step-10)

Let us consider each of these guidelines in more detail.

---

### Step 1: Start with the system, not a statistical model {#dag-step-1}

This is often the hardest part of constructing a DAG. Begin by thinking about the ecological system you are studying. Do not think about the regression or other model that you plan to fit. Do not think about whether you should log-transform a variable or not. At this point, focus on three questions:

* What are the major processes in this system? (e.g., predator-prey interactions, pollination, intrapair communication)
* What variables are likely to causally influence one another? (e.g., temperature and metabolic rate)
* What outcomes do I care about explaining? (e.g., fitness, probability of recruitment)

Again, at this first stage, your goal is to ignore anything related to statistical models. Do not worry about coefficients, significance, or functional form.

---

### Step 2: Identify your core exposure–outcome questions {#dag-step-2}

Next, write down the main causal questions you want the DAG to support. For example, consider the direct causal relationships I thought about *before* constructing the DAG above:

* What is the effect of $vegetation\_cover$ on $nesting\_survival$?
* What is the effect of $vegetation\_cover$ on $predator\_abundance$?
* What is the effect of $predator\_abundance$ on $nest\_concealment$?
* What is the effect of $predator\_abundance$ on $nesting\_survival$?
* What is the effect of $nest\_concealment$ on $nesting\_survival$?

These questions help identify important parts of the system that should be considered in the DAG.

---

### Step 3: Represent important causal relationships {#dag-step-3}

Begin making explicit causal claims about the relationships in your system. For example, if your question is:

> *What is the effect of $vegetation\_cover$ (the exposure) on $predator\_abundance$ (the outcome)?*

you might represent the hypothesized causal relationship as:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  vegetation_cover[Vegetation cover]:::exp --> predator_abundance[Predator abundance]:::out

classDef exp fill:#bcd4f6,color:#000,stroke-width:0px;
classDef out fill:#bfe3c0,color:#000,stroke-width:0px;
```

Even though this looks simple and almost trivial, be certain that each causal relationship is well justified. Every arrow you draw should be scientifically defensible based on some combination of theory, prior evidence, natural history, or observation.

A useful habit is to be able to complete the sentence:

> **I drew $A \rightarrow B$ because I hypothesize that changing $A$ could cause a change in $B$ because...**

The purpose here is not to connect variables simply because they were measured or because you expect them to be statistically related. The arrows represent your causal assumptions about how the study system operates.

---

### Step 4: Look upstream for common causes (confounders) {#dag-step-4}

Next, ask whether there are variables that could plausibly influence *both* an exposure and an outcome. Recall that these are called *confounders*, and they are often among the most important variables to identify.

For each candidate common cause, ask:

* Is there evidence (literature, pilot data, or natural history) that it affects $X$ (the exposure/treatment)?
* Is there evidence that it affects $Y$ (the response/outcome)?

When both relationships are justified, represent the common cause and the appropriate edges in your DAG:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  C["C (confounder)"]:::node --> X["X (exposure)"]:::node
  C --> Y["Y (outcome)"]:::node
  X --> Y

  classDef node fill:#9fbfe8,color:#000,stroke-width:0px;
```

At this stage, it is fine to include multiple potential common causes, but each edge—and its directionality—should still be grounded in scientific knowledge.

---

### Step 5: Look downstream for mechanisms and consequences {#dag-step-5}

This is where the utility of DAGs really shines. Ask whether the effect of $X$ on $Y$ operates through intermediate variables. These variables are called *mediators* and often represent ecological mechanisms.

For a causal question such as "does $X$ affect $Y$?", ask:

* *Through what variables might $X$ affect $Y$?*
* What other variables might be consequences of $X$?

For each candidate mediator, ask:

* Is there evidence that $X$ influences this variable?
* Is there evidence that this variable influences $Y$?

If both relationships are scientifically justified, add the mediator ($M$) to the DAG:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  C["C (confounder)"]:::node --> X["X (exposure)"]:::node
  C --> Y["Y (outcome)"]:::node
  X --> M["M (mediator)"]:::node
  M --> Y
  X --> Y

  classDef node fill:#9fbfe8,color:#000,stroke-width:0px;
```

Remember that mediators should represent real ecological or biological pathways and not just additional statistical covariates. If you ignore that distinction, you will be in the kitchen sink again.

---

### Step 6: Integrate the pieces into a common causal model {#dag-step-6}

As you construct the DAG, you will quickly notice that the same variables and pathways appear across multiple causal questions. This is a sign that you are capturing shared structure in the system rather than constructing isolated hypotheses.

Your goal is to integrate these overlapping pieces into a common causal model of the study system.

> **Start with a common causal model of the study system rather than constructing a new causal structure for each question. Different questions can focus attention on different exposure–outcome relationships within that common structure.**

When integrating the DAG, focus on:

* retaining variables that are relevant across multiple questions
* preserving pathways that are supported by scientific knowledge
* avoiding duplication of nodes that represent the same process
* including important latent variables where necessary

Importantly, each edge in this integrated DAG should still be defensible based on theory, literature, pilot data, natural history, or other scientific knowledge.

Don't worry if you forget something. DAG construction should be **iterative**. Expect to return to the graph and revise it as your understanding of the system improves.

---

### Step 7: Represent underlying processes (latent variables, measurement, and scale) {#dag-step-7}

At this stage, ask whether your DAG represents your best knowledge of the ecological process under study, or whether it represents only the variables you chose to measure out of convenience.

Hopefully, these lines of questioning occurred during the project-planning phase, where you could pre-emptively address three common issues that arise in ecological studies:

* **latent (unmeasured) variables**
* **scale and measurement**
* **proxy or index variables**

Of course, sometimes it is nearly impossible to anticipate all relevant ecological processes when you have not yet learned about a study system. Let us delve into these issues.

#### *Latent (unmeasured) variables* {#latent-variables}

What if we know that other factors matter—from prior literature, natural history knowledge, or previous studies—but we did not measure them in our own study? Sometimes a variable is not measured because it is logistically difficult to quantify, because there was insufficient funding, or because the variable's importance became clear only after the study was designed. **This situation is extremely common in ecology.**

Even when such variables are unmeasured, they can still play vital roles in the causal system (and your DAG representation of it). Exclusion of such a variable from your dataset does not remove it from the causal system. As such, it should be represented in the DAG as an unmeasured or *latent* variable (from Latin *latere*, meaning to "lie hidden").

A latent variable is simply a variable that:

* exists in the causal system
* influences other variables
* was not measured in your dataset

Examples can really include any variable, as long as it was not directly quantified in your study.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
### *Why include latent variables?*

Why exactly do I need to consider an unmeasured variable? This is where kitchen-sink modeling approaches can falter glamorously, as there is no explicit way to include such variables in the kinds of "garbage can regression" commonly used in ecology.

In Structural Causal Models, explicitly representing latent variables has three primary advantages:

* they help make your causal assumptions explicit
* they prevent incorrect adjustment decisions (and can help identify what kind of effect you are really estimating)
* they help identify unmeasured confounding and determine whether an effect is identifiable

:::


::: {.callout-warning icon=true collapse=false}

# Summary: Drawing only what you measured is a common mistake!

A very common mistake is to include only the measured variables in your dataset. This means that you are implicitly assuming that unmeasured variables do not matter. Entire books could be written on that assumption.

In reality, there are myriad important processes (e.g., habitat quality, predation risk) that may not have been measured. While unmeasured, they can still act as causal confounders. Structural Causal Models address this by allowing latent variables in the DAG.

:::


#### *Scale* {#dag-scale}

We know that different ecological processes are scale-dependent, so your "best knowledge" of your study system must also include information about the temporal and spatial scales at which you observed the system.

Ideally, process scale and measurement scale align, but in practice they often do not. The goal is to represent the data-generating structure as faithfully as possible and be transparent about your decisions.

Your "best knowledge" therefore includes not only the ecological processes in your study system, but also:

the spatial and temporal scale at which you think those processes actually operate
the spatial and temporal scale at which your variables were measured

How do we represent scale in a DAG? Recall that nodes represent variables (i.e., measured or unmeasured quantities). Scale is not itself a direct measurement that can cause something else. Because every variable is observed, inferred, or conceptualized at a particular spatial and temporal scale, scale should generally be embedded in the definition or measurement of the node.

Scale itself (e.g., a categorical variable for "large scale" or "small scale") should not appear as its own node in a DAG. For example, consider the same variable—precipitation—represented at different temporal scales:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  D[Daily precipitation]:::node --> M[Monthly precipitation]:::node
  D --> Y[Nesting success]:::node
  M --> Y

  classDef node fill:#9fbfe8,color:#000,stroke-width:0px;
```

Again, in this DAG, scale is not a separate node. Instead, it is embedded in how the variables are defined.

#### *Proxy or index variables* {#proxy-variables}

Another scenario occurs when the quantity that you measure is not the process itself. Rather, it is a small-scale (i.e. local) proxy for a broader-scale, unmeasured cause. Consider a study system where $territory_quality$ is an unmeasured (latent) variable operating at a broader scale, while $canopy_cover$ is a directly observed, local measurement:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  U[Territory quality]:::node --> X[Canopy cover]:::node
  U --> Y[Nesting success]:::node
  X --> Y

  classDef node fill:#9fbfe8,color:#000,stroke-width:0px;
```


::: {.callout-note icon=true}

Side note: Why does territory quality point to canopy cover?

In practice, we often use proxy or indicator measurements to characterize a broader conceptual quantity that we cannot measure directly. In this example, we might measure canopy cover at multiple subplots, perhaps along with variables such as humidity or insect abundance, and use these measurements secondarily as indicators of territory quality. Because we use the measurements to infer territory quality, it can be tempting to reverse the edge direction in the DAG.

However, a DAG represents the causal structure of the study system, not the direction in which we infer or calculate quantities from our data. In our example, territory quality represents broader, unmeasured ecological conditions associated with a territory—arising from processes such as soil, disturbance, and topography—that generate local characteristics we can measure, such as canopy cover.

Thus, the causal direction is territory quality → canopy cover even though we may use measured canopy cover to learn about territory quality. So, remember: Measurement order is not causal order:

- Territory quality: broader-scale latent condition
- Canopy cover: local measured proxy
- Nesting success: focal outcome

:::

---

### Step 8: Refine and interrogate the DAG

Now you have a solid draft DAG. Take a step back and carefully review it. This serves as a quality-control check on the causal assumptions represented in the graph.

Ask:

* Is every edge (arrow) clearly justified by scientific knowledge?
* Can I explain the causal reasoning behind every arrow?
* Are there important pathways missing based on prior knowledge?
* Are there important common causes that I have omitted?
* Should some variables be represented as unmeasured (latent) rather than observed?
* Are the directions of the arrows temporally and biologically plausible?
* Does this DAG represent the system as I think it actually operates, rather than simply the hypothesis or result I would prefer?

Careful and transparent refinement is where the DAG becomes more than a back-of-the-napkin sketch; it becomes a scientifically defensible representation of your causal assumptions about the study system. Keep your napkin sketch, though, as you might need it again one day. 

At this stage, a large DAG represents a defensible hypothesis about what causes what in your study system. The DAG now represents a huge amount of knowledge packed into a relatively small graph. The next step is to consider how those causes combine, including whether the effect of one variable depends on the level of another.

---

## Step 9: Consider effect modification (interactions)

The last effect type in our causal framework is the effect modifier. An effect modifier is a variable that makes the effect of $X$ on $Y$ depend on another variable $Z$. In practice, this is what we mean by an interaction (a term familiar to you from GLMs and GLMMs).

Conceptually, it really is that simple. For example, predator abundance may reduce nesting success, but the strength of that effect may depend on vegetation structure. In a DAG, this is represented simply as both $predator_abundance$ and $vegetation_structure$ causing $nesting_survival$:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR

X[Predator abundance]:::exp_dark --> Y[Nest survival]:::out
Z[Vegetation structure]:::exp_light --> Y

classDef exp_dark fill:#9fbfe8,color:#000,stroke-width:0px;
classDef exp_light fill:#d6e6fb,color:#000,stroke-width:0px;
classDef out fill:#bfe3c0,color:#000,stroke-width:0px;
```

What does this show? Both predator abundance and vegetation structure affect nest survival. Effect modification arises when the effect of predator abundance on survival depends on vegetation structure (an interaction). The DAG itself does not change. That is, effect modification does not introduce a new causal relationship—it changes how existing causes combine in the structural model for $Y$. This raises an important question: *where does the interaction appear, as it is not explicitly encoded in the DAG?*

Remember that a DAG shows which variables are causes of $Y$. The DAG does not specify how those causes combine, whether additively or interactively. Instead, the interaction appears in the structural equation:

$$ Y \sim X + Z + X \times Z $$

Here, the $X \times Z$ term means that the effect of $X$ on $Y$ depends on the value of $Z$. After building your DAG, carefully document how variables will enter your structural models, including hypothesized interactions and random effects.
---

## Step 10: Use the DAG to determine what questions are possible

This is one of the most fascinating and fun parts of DAG construction. We will discuss this in greater detail in coming weeks. 

A well-constructed DAG does more than simply represent the causal assumptions underlying your original hypotheses and questions. It allows you to systematically evaluate what questions can be supported by the causal structure you have represented.

You can now narrow your focus onto questions such as:

* Which exposure–outcome relationships are supported by plausible causal pathways?
* Which variables play multiple roles across different questions?
* Which effects are identifiable or unidentifiable given the causal structure?
* What new questions emerge from the causal structure?

Remember that you are formalizing the causal assumptions of your study system. This can be done before, during, or after a study, though it is ideal to begin **before** the study whenever possible.

Our understanding of an ecological system will often change as we study it. We conduct experiments, make observations, read new and old literature, and speak with colleagues. Therefore, we should expect the DAG to evolve over time.

Keeping the DAG updated as our scientific understanding changes can help us identify where past studies have fallen short, what present studies are constrained to estimate, and what future studies should prioritize.
````
